question: Mbaaɗa. Mi yi'i white powdery coating on leaves e la'ano am. Ɗume rafi woni ɗo'o?
answer: powdery mildew woni rafi bonnata ndemri maa. Ɗum saakitoo e fungus spreads in dry season. Nyawndam: spray sulfur fungicide. remove infected leaves.

question: Ụtụtụ ọma. Ahụrụ m sores in mouth and on hooves na mmiri ara m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?
answer: foot and mouth disease (FMD) na-emebi ihe ọkụkụ gị. Ọ na-agbasa site na highly contagious viral disease. Ngwọta: isolate infected animals. call veterinarian immediately.
source: NRCRI Umudike, disease diagnosis advisory for dairy farmers

question: Ndewo. Ahụrụ m white fuzzy growth on leaves na yorobo m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?

source: NRCRI Umudike, disease diagnosis advisory for onion farmers

question: Eku oo, mo ri pe awon ewe sorghum mi ti n are showing signs of striga weed. Kini ohun ti mo le se lati gba to?
answer: Eyi je kokoro sorghum shoot fly. Esinsin yi n yin eyin si ori ewe kekere, idin re si n wo inu igi. Imoran: gbin ni kutukutu, tabi lo irugbin ti o lagbara bi SAMSORG 40.
source: NAERLS-Extension, pest/disease advisory for sorghum farmers

question: Sannu da aiki. auduga ta na da matsala — larvae bore into bolls causing them to drop. Wane irin kwaro ne wannan kuma me zan yi?

source: NAERLS-Zaria, pest management advisory for cotton farmers

question: Se dada ni. Mo ri wipe kofi mi ni small holes in coffee berries with damage inside. Iru kokoro wo ni eyi ati kini mo le se?
answer: coffee berry borer (Hypothenemus hampei) lo n damu oko re. most serious coffee pest globally. Ohun ti o ye ki o se: harvest all ripe berries promptly. Ma gbagbe — use broca traps with ethanol-methanol mix.
source: IAR&T Obafemi Awolowo University, pest management advisory for coffee farmers

question: Daalunu. yam m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: The yellow-green leaf pattern you describe is Cassava Mosaic Disease caused by geminiviruses transmitted by whiteflies. There is no chemical cure. (1) Uproot and burn ALL affected plants immediately — do NOT use them as planting material. (2) Use certified mosaic-resistant varieties: TME 419, TMS 30572, or IITA-TMS-I011412. (3) Plant stakes at the recommended spacing of 1 m × 1 m. (4) Avoid recycling stakes from infected fields. (5) Intercrop with maize or cowpea to reduce whitefly populations. Contact your nearest IITA or NRCRI extension office for free resistant planting material.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnọọ. ose m nwere nsogbu — fruits rot from inside with maggots. Kedu ụdị ahụhụ nke a bụ, gịnị ka m ga-eme?

source: ILRI/IAR Samaru, pest management advisory for millet farmers

question: Mo ni iṣoro pẹlu plantain mi, awon ewe re ni awon aami bi mosaic lori ewe, ko si dagba daradara. Jowo ran mi lowo.

question: Sannu. rice na ba ya girma sosai, ganye suna bushewa. Me zan yi?
answer: Oval brown spots on leaves indicate brown spot (Cochliobolus miyabeanus), often associated with nutrient deficiency, especially silicon. (1) Apply potassium silicate at 2 ml/L foliar spray — this strengthens leaf cell walls. (2) Apply balanced NPK (15-15-15) at 200 kg/ha if the crop appears yellowish overall. (3) Spray propiconazole at 1 ml/L if spots cover >10% of leaf area. (4) Avoid water stress — maintain 2-5 cm standing water. (5) For the next season, incorporate rice husks into the soil to increase silicon availability.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo maize m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Chlorotic streaks following leaf veins indicate Maize Streak Virus transmitted by leafhoppers (Cicadulina spp.). There is no cure. (1) Remove and destroy all affected plants immediately. (2) Plant early at the onset of rains to avoid peak leafhopper populations. (3) Use streak-resistant hybrids: ZM 623, SC 627, or WH 505. (4) Do not plant maize near irrigated vegetable fields, which harbor leafhoppers year-round. (5) Apply carbofuran granules at 1.5 kg a.i./ha to the soil at planting to control early-season vectors. (6) Save seed only from completely disease-free plants.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Mo ni isoro pelu tomato mi, awon ewe re ni awon kokoro funfun lori ewe. Jowo ran mi lowo.
answer: Fine webbing and yellow stippling on leaves indicate spider mites (Tetranychus spp.), which thrive in hot, dry conditions. (1) Spray the underside of leaves with a strong jet of water every 3 days to dislodge mites and break webbing. (2) Apply micronized sulfur at 3 g/L or abamectin at 0.5 ml/L. (3) Avoid pyrethroids and broad-spectrum insecticides — they kill predatory mites and trigger mite explosions. (4) Increase humidity around plants by mulching and watering the ground (not leaves) in the morning. (5) For heavy infestation, release Phytoseiulus persimilis predatory mites — 10/m².
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. yam m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit indicate anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.). (1) Remove and destroy all infected plant parts — do NOT compost them. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L or mancozeb at 2.5 g/L every 10-14 days, starting at flowering. (3) Prune to improve air circulation and reduce humidity. (4) Apply 2-3 cm of organic mulch to prevent rain splash. (5) For the next season, use certified disease-free seed and practice 3-year crop rotation with cereals. Pre-harvest interval: 7-14 days depending on the product.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Furen rana (sunflower) na ganye suna yin launin ruwan kasa. Cutace ne?

(3) Yi maganin iri da ruwan zafi (52°C) na mintuna 10 kafin shuka. (4) Yi amfani da mai na neem (neem oil 5ml/lita). (5) Juya amfanin gona — kada a shuka furen rana a gona guda kowace shekara. (6) Tuntuɓi jami'in noma don ƙarin shawara.

question: Wake na suna da tsutsotsi a ciki. Yadda za a ajiye su?

question: Sannu. mango na suna yin rawaya tare da bakaken tabo. Me zan yi?
answer: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit indicate anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.). (1) Remove and destroy all infected plant parts — do NOT compost them. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L or mancozeb at 2.5 g/L every 10-14 days, starting at flowering. (3) Prune to improve air circulation and reduce humidity. (4) Apply 2-3 cm of organic mulch to prevent rain splash. (5) For the next season, use certified disease-free seed and practice 3-year crop rotation with cereals. Pre-harvest interval: 7-14 days depending on the product.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Ina fama da matsalar oil palm ta. Ganyayyakin sun suna yin rawaya tare da bakaken tabo. Yaya zan magance wannan?
answer: Yellowing patterns on oil palm indicate nutrient deficiency. (1) For nitrogen deficiency (uniform yellowing of older leaves): apply urea at 1-2 kg per tree per year, split into 2 applications. (2) For potassium deficiency (orange spotting on older leaves): apply muriate of potash at 2-3 kg per tree per year. (3) For magnesium deficiency (yellowing between veins of older leaves): apply kieserite at 0.5-1 kg per tree. (4) Apply empty fruit bunch (EFB) mulch at 60 t/ha around palms — it slowly releases nutrients. (5) Conduct a leaf analysis (take leaf #17 from 20 palms) to confirm which nutrients are deficient before large-scale fertiliser application.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Ina fama da matsalar banana ta. Ganyayyakin sun suna da kananan kwari akan ganye. Yaya zan magance wannan?
answer: Upright, crowded leaves with a 'bunchy' appearance and dark green streaking on petioles indicate Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) transmitted by the banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa). (3) Never use suckers from an affected field for new plantings. (4) Use tissue-culture plantlets — they are guaranteed virus-free. (5) Contact your agricultural extension office to report BBTV — it is a notifiable disease in most countries. (6) Quarantine any new planting material for 4 weeks.

question: Ezigbo ụbọchị. Achọrọ m ịmata otu m ga-esi groundnut planting n'ugbo akidi m. Gịnị ka ị ga-adụ m ọdụ?
answer: Nke a bụ ndụmọdụ m maka groundnut planting na akidi: sow seeds 5cm deep. Nke a na-enyere aka n'ihi na space 60cm between rows, 15cm between plants. groundnut needs well-drained sandy loam soil.

question: Eku oo, cassava mi ti n di ofeefee pelu awon abawon dudu. Kini mo le se?
answer: This is cassava whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Do NOT spray broad-spectrum insecticides — they kill natural enemies like Encarsia wasps and make outbreaks worse. Instead: (1) Spray insecticidal soap or 0.5% neem oil solution every 7 days for 3 weeks. (2) Remove and burn heavily infested leaves. (3) Plant maize or sorghum as barrier crops between cassava rows to disrupt whitefly movement. (4) Use yellow sticky traps (1 per 10 m²). If infestation persists, apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L as a LAST resort, observing a 14-day pre-harvest interval. Wash hands and produce after application.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Sannu. plantain na suna da kananan kwari akan ganye. Me zan yi?
answer: Dark brown streaks that enlarge to black spots on leaves indicate Black Sigatoka (Mycosphaerella fijiensis). This disease can reduce yield by 50%+. (1) Remove and destroy all heavily infected leaves — do NOT leave them on the ground. (2) Spray propiconazole at 1 ml/L OR difenoconazole at 0.5 ml/L every 14-21 days during the rainy season. ALTERNATE fungicides to prevent resistance. (3) Improve drainage — standing water increases spore production. (4) Reduce planting density for better airflow (standard: 1,700 plants/ha; reduce to 1,400 if disease is severe). (5) De-leaf weekly, leaving only 8-10 functional leaves per plant.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Ụtụtụ ọma. Ahụrụ m white powder on flowers and leaves na kashu m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?

question: E ku agba mi. Mo ri yellow streaks on leaves lori agbado mi. Arun wo ni eyi?

question: Assalamu alaikum. Ina so in san yadda zan cabbage planting a aikin kabeji don in samu riba mai kyau. Me za ku ce?

question: Nnọọ. tii m nwere nsogbu — dark spots on leaves and young shoots. Kedu ụdị ahụhụ nke a bụ, gịnị ka m ga-eme?

question: Assalamu alaikum. Na ga dark spots on leaves and vine dieback a jikin doya ta. Wace cuta ce wannan?

question: Se dada ni. Mo ri wipe pakí mi ni leaves appear bunched and distorted. Iru kokoro wo ni eyi ati kini mo le se?

question: Ina fama da matsalar cotton ta. Ganyayyakin sun suna yin rawaya tare da bakaken tabo. Yaya zan magance wannan?
answer: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown indicate bacterial blight (Xanthomonas spp.). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L + streptomycin at 0.3 g/L at first sign. (2) Avoid working in the field when plants are wet — bacteria spread through water. (3) Use only acid-delinted, certified seed. (4) Rotate with maize or sorghum for 2-3 years. (5) Remove and burn all crop residues after harvest. (6) Avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes lush, susceptible growth.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Barka dai. Na ga dark spots on ripening fruit a jikin mangwaro ta. Wace cuta ce wannan?

source: NAERLS/ABU Zaria, disease diagnosis advisory for mango farmers

question: Sannu da zuwa. barkono ta na da matsala — fruits rot from inside with maggots. Wane irin kwaro ne wannan kuma me zan yi?

question: Ezigbo ụbọchị. watermelon m nwere nsogbu — larvae inside fruit causing rot. Kedu ụdị ahụhụ nke a bụ, gịnị ka m ga-eme?
answer: melon fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) na-akpata nsogbu n'ubi gị. fly punctures fruit to lay eggs. Ihe ị ga-eme: cover young fruits with paper bags. Echefula — harvest early before pest builds up.

question: Mo ni isoro pelu watermelon mi, awon ewe re ko dagba daradara, ewe re ti rerun. Jowo ran mi lowo.
answer: Soft spots on fruit with small puncture marks and larvae (maggots) inside indicate fruit fly (Bactrocera / Ceratitis spp.). (1) Collect ALL fallen and infested fruit daily — place them in a sealed black plastic bag and leave in the sun for 7 days to kill larvae. (2) Use methyl eugenol pheromone traps (1 trap per 0.1 ha). (3) Apply GF-120 (Spinosad-based fruit fly bait) as spot sprays on a small patch of leaves — do NOT spray the fruit. (4) Bag individual fruits with paper bags when they reach half-size. (5) Plough the soil under the tree canopy to expose pupae. (6) NEVER use unapproved systemic insecticides on fruit crops.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Odidẹ (sunflower) mi ko so eso daradara. Kini iṣoro?

question: Daalunu. onion m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Soft, rotting bulb base with white fungal growth indicates basal rot (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae). (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — do NOT store bulbs from infected rows. (2) Treat seed bulbs with Trichoderma viride (10 g/kg seed) before planting. (3) Avoid injury to bulbs during weeding. (4) Harvest when 50% of tops have fallen and cure bulbs in the sun for 7-10 days. (5) Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. (6) Rotate away from alliums for 4 years.

question: Daalunu. cocoa m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Sunken, black lesions on young shoots and pods indicate mirids/capsids (Sahlbergella singularis). (1) Spray imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L OR bifenthrin at 1 ml/L, targeting the canopy thoroughly. (5) Monitor weekly with a beating tray or by tapping branches over a white cloth to count insects. Treat when you find >4 mirids per 10 taps.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

answer: bean fly (Ophiomyia phaseoli) lo n damu oko re. fly larvae bore into stems. Ohun ti o ye ki o se: plant early to escape peak fly season. Ma gbagbe — apply mulch around plants.
source: IAR&T Obafemi Awolowo University, pest management advisory for beans farmers

question: Eku agba mi, groundnut mi ni awon kokoro funfun lori ewe. Kini o ye ki n se nitori ki n le gba ikore?
answer: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaves indicate rust (Puccinia spp.). (1) Spray propiconazole at 1 ml/L OR tebuconazole at 0.5 ml/L at first sign. (2) Plant resistant varieties where available. (3) Avoid excessive nitrogen — it promotes lush, susceptible growth. (4) Remove and destroy crop residues after harvest. (5) Practice early planting to avoid peak rust season. (6) Apply balanced NPK (not just urea) to strengthen cell walls.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Ụtụtụ ọma. Ahụrụ m diamond-shaped gray lesions on leaves na osikapa m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?
answer: rice blast (Pyricularia oryzae) na-emebi ihe ọkụkụ gị. Ọ na-agbasa site na fungal spores carried by wind. Ngwọta: use resistant varieties like FARO 44. excess nitrogen makes blast worse.
source: NRCRI Umudike, disease diagnosis advisory for rice farmers

question: E ku ise. Mo ri wipe gbogiri mi ni larvae inside fruit causing rot. Iru kokoro wo ni eyi ati kini mo le se?
answer: melon fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) lo n damu oko re. fly punctures fruit to lay eggs. Ohun ti o ye ki o se: cover young fruits with paper bags. Ma gbagbe — harvest early before pest builds up.
source: IAR&T Obafemi Awolowo University, pest management advisory for watermelon farmers

question: Ututu oma. tii m nwere nsogbu — shoot tips wilt and die back. Kedu ụdị ahụhụ nke a bụ, gịnị ka m ga-eme?
answer: Nke a bụ ahụhụ a na-akpọ tea mosquito bug. bug injects toxin during feeding. Ngwọta: shade regulation reduces population. Echefula — neem-based sprays for organic control.
source: NRCRI-Umudike, pest management advisory for tea farmers

question: Bawo ni o. Mo ri dark greasy spots on leaves and fruit rot lori tomatii mi. Arun wo ni eyi?
answer: Eyi je arun ti a mo si late blight (Phytophthora infestans). O n tan kaakiri nipase fungus thrives in cool wet weather. rotate tomatoes away from potato fields. Ohun ti o ye ki o se: spray mancozeb preventively. rotate tomatoes away from potato fields.
source: IAR&T-Ibadan, disease diagnosis advisory for tomato farmers

question: Daalunu. plantain m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Holes at the base of the pseudostem and wilting plants indicate banana/plantain weevil borer (Cosmopolites sordidus). (1) Set up pseudostem traps: cut a 30 cm piece of harvested stem, split it lengthwise, and place it cut-side down near the plant. Check and destroy trapped weevils every 2 days. (2) Apply neem cake at 100 g per plant around the base. (3) Remove old, harvested stems at ground level — they are breeding sites. (4) For heavy infestation, drench the soil around the base with chlorpyrifos at 2 ml/L (wear gloves and avoid runoff into water sources). (5) Use clean, weevil-free suckers for the next planting.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Mo ni isoro pelu plantain mi, awon ewe re ko dagba daradara, ewe re ti rerun. Jowo ran mi lowo.
answer: Stunted growth, yellowing, swollen root galls (knots), and wilting despite moist soil indicate root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.). (1) There is no curative chemical treatment. (2) Incorporate fresh neem leaves or neem cake at 500 kg/ha into the soil 2 weeks before the next planting. (3) Solarize the soil with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks. (4) Plant marigold (Tagetes erecta) as a trap crop — its roots release natural nematicides. (5) Rotate with maize, sorghum, or millet for 2-3 seasons — these are non-hosts. (6) Apply well-composted manure at 5 t/ha; the microbial activity suppresses nematodes.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Barka dai. Na ga yellow leaves with white underside a jikin sunflower ta. Wace cuta ce wannan?
answer: downy mildew ce ke cutar amfanin gonar ka. Tana yaduwa ta hanyar fungus survives in soil. Magani: use resistant varieties. rotate crops for 3 years.

question: Ndewo. Ahụrụ m leaves become narrow and bunched at top na unere m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo rice m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Oval brown spots on leaves indicate brown spot (Cochliobolus miyabeanus), often associated with nutrient deficiency, especially silicon. (1) Apply potassium silicate at 2 ml/L foliar spray — this strengthens leaf cell walls. (2) Apply balanced NPK (15-15-15) at 200 kg/ha if the crop appears yellowish overall. (3) Spray propiconazole at 1 ml/L if spots cover >10% of leaf area. (4) Avoid water stress — maintain 2-5 cm standing water. (5) For the next season, incorporate rice husks into the soil to increase silicon availability.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Bawo ni. Mo fe mo bi mo se le banana planting fun oko ogede mi. Kini imoran re?
answer: Eyi ni imoran mi lori banana planting fun ogede: plant healthy suckers 30cm deep. Eyi yoo se iranlowo nitori pe space 3m between plants. water regularly during dry season.

question: No wa'i. Miɗo yiɗi anndude no mi waɗirta groundnut planting e ndemri biriiji am. Ɗume wasiyiiji maa?
answer: Wasiyanke am dow groundnut planting e biriiji: sow seeds 5cm deep. Ɗum wallitata sabo space 60cm between rows, 15cm between plants. groundnut needs well-drained sandy loam soil.
source: ILRI/IAR Samaru, cultural practice advisory for groundnut farmers

question: Nnọọ. Achọrọ m ịmata otu m ga-esi okra planting n'ugbo okwuru m. Gịnị ka ị ga-adụ m ọdụ?
answer: Nke a bụ ndụmọdụ m maka okra planting na okwuru: sow seeds 2-3cm deep. Nke a na-enyere aka n'ihi na space 60cm between rows, 30cm between plants. okra needs full sun and well-drained soil.
source: NRCRI Umudike, cultural practice advisory for okra farmers

question: Ezigbo ụbọchị. Achọrọ m ịmata otu m ga-esi amaranth planting n'ugbo green m. Gịnị ka ị ga-adụ m ọdụ?
answer: Nke a bụ ndụmọdụ m maka amaranth planting na green: broadcast seeds on prepared bed. Nke a na-enyere aka n'ihi na water regularly. harvest after 4-6 weeks.

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo cotton m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Yellowing leaves that wilt during the day and internal stem browning indicate Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum). Once a plant shows symptoms, it cannot be saved. (1) Uproot and burn the affected plant with its root ball — do NOT compost. (2) Drench the planting hole with Trichoderma viride (10 g/L) + lime (50 g/hole). (3) Do NOT plant susceptible crops in that spot for 3-4 years — rotate with maize or rice. (4) Solarize the soil during the hottest months. (5) Use resistant varieties (FHIA series for banana). (6) Always use tissue-culture plantlets or certified disease-free suckers for new plantings — the fungus persists in infected planting material.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Ndewo. Ahụrụ m dark streaks on leaves reducing photosynthesis na ogidi m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?
answer: black sigatoka (Mycosphaerella fijiensis) na-emebi ihe ọkụkụ gị. Ọ na-agbasa site na fungus spread by wind. Ngwọta: spray fungicide regularly. remove infected leaves.
source: NRCRI Umudike, disease diagnosis advisory for plantain farmers

question: Sannu da zuwa. Na ga white powder on leaves reducing photosynthesis a jikin kankana ta. Wace cuta ce wannan?
answer: Wannan cuta ce da ake kira powdery mildew on watermelon. Yana yaduwa ta hanyar thrives in dry warm weather. plant resistant hybrid varieties. Abin yi: sulfur spray at first sign. plant resistant hybrid varieties.

question: Ututu oma. kashu m nwere nsogbu — grub bores into trunk causing branch dieback. Kedu ụdị ahụhụ nke a bụ, gịnị ka m ga-eme?

question: Daalu o. Ahụrụ m rectangular gray spots on lower leaves na oka m. Kedu ọrịa nke a bụ?
answer: Nke a bụ ọrịa a na-akpọ gray leaf spot. Ọ na-agbasa site na fungal spores in soil debris. thrives in warm humid conditions. Ihe ị ga-eme: fungicide spray (mancozeb). thrives in warm humid conditions.

question: Makkabe am na markooje (lodging). Ko waɗi?
answer: Makkabe ɗe markooje ko stem borers mbaɗi. (1) Lartu makkabe ɗe markii — suna. (2) Demoo ko adii — borers ɗen keƴaako. (3) Luurtin ndema — woto a demoo makkabe e ngesa goota hitaande fof. (4) Demoo gabbe ɗe ngooɗata: 'SC 403', 'MH 30'. (5) Huutoro neem oil (5ml/lita) nder makka. (6) Yeewtu e ADP ngam insecticide approved.
source: ADP Maize Borer Guide; CIMMYT Borer Management

question: Ndewo. ose m nwere nsogbu — fruits rot from inside with maggots. Kedu ụdị ahụhụ nke a bụ, gịnị ka m ga-eme?
answer: pepper fruit fly (Bactrocera latifrons) na-akpata nsogbu n'ubi gị. fly punctures fruit to lay eggs. Ihe ị ga-eme: harvest regularly before pest builds up. Echefula — bag young fruits with paper.

question: Eku oo, cowpea mi ti n di ofeefee pelu awon abawon dudu. Kini mo le se?
answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. (1) Spray insecticidal soap (5 ml liquid soap in 1 L water) directly on the insects every 3 days. (2) Strong water spray can dislodge light infestations. (3) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (4) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings, and hoverflies — plant marigold or coriander near cowpea to attract them. (5) If infestation is severe and ants are present (ants farm aphids), apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. Remove ants with a sticky barrier around plant stems first.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo rice m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Bronze-orange discolouration of older leaves ("bronzing") indicates iron toxicity, common in waterlogged, acidic soils. (1) Drain the field for 3-5 days to aerate the soil — this allows iron to precipitate out of the soil solution. (2) Apply lime (2-4 t/ha) to raise soil pH above 5.0. (3) Use NPK 15-15-15 fertiliser rather than single-nutrient fertilisers — potassium helps reduce iron uptake. (4) Plant tolerant varieties: NERICA-L series or TOX 4004. (5) In the next season, avoid continuous flooding of young seedlings; use alternate wetting and drying irrigation.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature
